In 1987, Nobel Prize–winning economist Robert Solow wrote, “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.”

The same could be said about AI today.

Gartner projects worldwide AI spending of $2.59 trillion in 2026 , a 47% jump over last year, with the US accounting for at least half that amount, according to a wide range of estimates.

But in the US, utilization-adjusted total factor productivity grew just 0.07% over the four quarters ending in the first quarter of 2026 . That is a near-standstill by historical standards, far below the roughly half-percent annual pace typical of the pre-ChatGPT decade.

Some 95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots have produced no measurable effect on the bottom line .

A report published this week found that even Meta, one of AI’s loudest boosters, has fallen short in its plan to replace workers with AI .

The question of the decade is: Why?

## One idea: Blame users

A working paper posted to SSRN by University of Pittsburgh business professor Mark Ma and colleagues, makes a sweeping claim: The productivity shortfall is caused by employees who resist AI out of fear for their jobs.

Over a five-year period, the researchers looked at millions of Glassdoor reviews, thousands of financial reports, hundreds of AI-investment and layoff announcements by US public companies, and some 10,000 earnings-call transcripts.

They found a wide divide between managers, who tend to be true believers in the promise that AI will deliver sky-high productivity, and employees, who worry that AI-driven productivity gains will cost them their jobs.

Companies, the researchers claim, are caught in a doom loop in which they lay off employees, citing productivity gains. But fear of layoffs causes workers to resist the technology, which sabotages the very gains the companies were counting on. Executives see that lack of productivity and conclude that more layoffs will help. (The flogging will continue until morale improves….)

It’s a tidy narrative. There’s just one problem — while parts of this study are backed by verifiable data, two key elements are not. The report fails to support their assumption that fear of layoffs causes employees to resist using AI, and also that productivity gains would be higher if only workers would enthusiastically embrace it.

The researchers never establish causation in their data. It’s a correlation. (That hasn’t stopped other outlets from reporting the link as causal.)

(A quick aside: One of my favorite podcasters, the economist Tyler Cowen, flagged a study this week that examined 194,631 cross-sectional social science papers and found that the share using causal language in titles or abstracts rose from a stable 20% before 2000 to more than 60% by 2024. Unproven causal claims appear to be something of a fad in social science .)

I don’t buy the claim that employee foot-dragging explains the missing productivity gains, for one simple reason: It makes no sense.

For starters, the notion that rank-and-file employees are broadly resisting AI isn’t entirely true. Many are embracing it. A Columbia Business School survey of 1,400 US employees, written up in Harvard Business Review , found that 31% of individual contributors expressed enthusiasm about adopting AI. And many of the non-enthusiastic are being forced to embrace it. More than half of US workers now use AI.

If AI is a significant driver of productivity, businesses should generally be seeing measurable gains now that roughly half of US workers report using it on the job.

Another issue: Workers who think AI might take their jobs have every incentive not to avoid it but to use it conspicuously, demonstrating that they’re on board with the company’s pro-AI policy.

I think the more likely explanation involves another dynamic altogether.

## A better idea: Blame AI overload

The time and trouble of producing a business report, proposal, plan, slide deck, or budget used to limit how large, how complex, and how frequent such documents were. Now, thanks to AI, people can churn out incredibly complex business communications, ideas, and proposals in a few minutes.

Using AI makes the person generating such documents super productive. But then it burdens everyone else who has to sift through those documents, teasing out hallucinations, problems, and irrelevancies, and struggling to grasp ideas that even the so-called creator hasn’t taken the time to understand.

One person’s productivity is everyone else’s information overload, lowering a company’s overall productivity.

“AI can make an organization extraordinarily busy without necessarily making it more productive,” said Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, in the report on Meta I mentioned above.

This dynamic is playing out everywhere:

- Job applicants can use AI to apply for far more positions, burdening hiring managers and slowing the hiring process. (LinkedIn data shows applications per job posting in the US have roughly doubled since spring 2022.) AI that’s supposed to make it easier to find a job actually makes it harder.

- AI is emboldening more people to represent themselves in court while also speeding up the work of lawyers. A 2026 study by researchers at MIT and USC drew on 4.5 million federal civil cases filed between 2005 and 2026, applied an AI-text detector to a random sample of 1,600 complaints, and found that the share containing AI-generated text rose from 1% in 2023 to 18% in early 2026. That burdens judges, who now have to comb through long, complex filings for citations to nonexistent cases and other hallucinations, slowing justice. AI that’s supposed to make court cases quicker makes them slower.

- Students increasingly use AI to produce longer essays, and a growing number of instructors report leaning on AI tools to keep up with grading, a loop in which the writing and the reading are both partly automated.

AI-pilled chatbot enthusiasts who believe the technology is solving all their problems are judging AI through a narrow personal lens. Likewise, analysts and AI companies look at one person’s productivity gains, extrapolate across thousands of employees, and wrongly conclude that the gains will scale without considering the impact of that output on the productivity of others.

## Understanding the problem at scale

The idea that productivity-enhancing AI might reduce productivity sounds paradoxical, so consider this oversimplified thought experiment. Suppose AI enables you to write three times as many emails as before (say, 30 a day instead of 10). Your email-writing productivity has tripled, making you more valuable to the company.

The problem is that every additional email you send lands in someone else’s inbox. Your colleagues, who once got 10 emails from you daily, now get 30. Multiply that across an organization: if 10 people triple their email output, the team gets 300 emails a day instead of 100. If 100 people do the same, that figure blows up to 3,000, three times the reading burden. The AI that makes email writing easy makes email reading hard for everyone else.

Of course, this dynamic doesn’t apply to every use of AI, every industry, or every employee.

But on the macro level, this is clearly happening. I’m sure you’ve seen it at your own company. And it helps explain what Deloitte called the “paradox of rising investment and elusive returns.”

AI isn’t “bad.” But shortsighted and delusional thinking about it is.

AI is like nearly every powerful technology since the Industrial Revolution: It rewards individuals for behavior that collectively exhausts a shared resource (in this case, human attention).

What’s called for is a wholesale redesign of workplace AI. We need tools built not to make the individual user more “productive,” but to make the organization more productive, magnifying individual ability without dumping needless work on everyone else.

According to a new study by the research firm Forrester, AI will account for 20% of corporate technology spending in 2027. At the same time, more than half of IT executives are expected to miss their return-on-investment targets, reports The Register .

In the survey, 45% of AI decision-makers state that investments must yield a positive return within one year to be considered successful. At the same time, only 22% have seen a positive impact on their company’s operating profit over the past year.

According to Forrester, the problems stem in part from companies investing in AI technology without simultaneously changing their organizations and work processes. Instead, the financial gains are realized within individual use cases.

To keep costs down, companies are expected to increasingly use open AI models in the future, as they are cheaper to operate. More expensive and advanced AI models are expected to be reserved for more critical tasks.

We talk to chatbots as if those conversations are private. But are they?

Most people are confused. A survey commissioned by DuckDuckGo and published in August asked 1,944 American adults about chatbot privacy, and more than half (53%) did not know whether their conversations were being used to train the bots. (They are.)

Only a quarter of respondents knew that chatbot conversations can be subpoenaed. (They can.)

Among self-described AI enthusiasts, 56% said they had confided to a chatbot something they had never told a close friend, parent, colleague, doctor, or therapist.

That’s especially true on Character.AI, a chatbot service where users can chat and form “relationships” with customizable characters, including ones they create and share with the community. On Character.AI, some users chat about thoughts of suicide and self-harm, and they surrender private details like mental health disclosures, ages, private chats and voice calls, deep fears, and relationship struggles.

Character.AI was all fun and games until earlier this month, when the company filed for bankruptcy and opened a court-supervised sale of its assets.

Nobody knows who will end up with the company, or how much of the data on its millions of account holders will be sold as well.

The most valuable asset for sale by the company may be its LLM, which has been substantially trained by users as they build and interact with characters.

Legally, a company can sell personal data about its users if its privacy policy permits the transfer. Character.AI’s privacy policy is spectacularly vague. It says the company may disclose “certain information” in the company’s sale. Nobody knows what that means.

The US Trustee Office, an arm of the Justice Department, wants the judge to appoint a consumer privacy ombudsman to advise the court on user privacy. The judge could restrict the sale of company “records,” including user data.

But here’s the part most people don’t understand: The Bankruptcy Code has no provision specifically addressing trained models. The legal status of LLMs and their training data has yet to be settled in law. That means it’s entirely possible that the data users fed into Character.AI will be sold to whoever buys it.

Character.AI is just one handy example. The larger risk is all the other AI companies out there.

## More surprising facts about LLM privacy

The core question is this: Can personal or proprietary information shared in a chat end up inside an LLM, where anyone might coax it out?

The answer is a resounding “uh, maybe.”

First of all, it depends on the AI chatbot service. The companies vary wildly in how they handle chat data, and the differences boil down to four questions: whether training on chats is on by default, whether human reviewers read them, how long they are kept, and whether they feed advertising.

Major chatbot companies generally try to reassure users about privacy. They publish privacy controls, but their own policies admit that consumer chats may be used for training by default, read by human reviewers, or both, and the fine print shifts from company to company.

Tellingly, some of them offer enterprise or business accounts that handle chat sessions privately. For example, they don’t use chat sessions in training data. That business accounts get extra privacy features sounds to me like an admission that individual accounts aren’t private.

Some companies, such as OpenAI, let users opt out of having their chats tossed into the training data. But OpenAI’s help documentation says that turning off training does not delete the chats themselves.

There are three main ways chatbot user data can be exposed. The first is bugs. In March 2023, a bug lurking in an open-source library called “redis-py” let some ChatGPT users see other users’ chat titles and, possibly, the first message of new conversations. More than 1% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have had their payment details exposed to other users: names, email addresses, payment addresses, card types, the last four digits of card numbers and expiration dates.

The second is sharing. Some chatbots offer sharing features, and those features can publish chats to the world, whether on purpose or by accident. Once these sessions are posted, search engines are likely to gobble them up and make them searchable. In 2025, Forbes reported that Google’s results showed more than 370,000 Grok conversations after users clicked “share,” and shared ChatGPT chats turned up in search results until OpenAI killed the option.

The third is the absorption of chat sessions into the training data.

Let’s take one simple example: an email address. People often paste in emails so that a chatbot will write the reply. These emails often contain names, email addresses and other information in the header, the signature, or both.

The question I often ponder is this: If emails addressed to one person get pasted into chats hundreds of times, can a stranger ask the chatbot for that person’s address and actually get it back?

In a 2022 study , GPT-Neo models given only a person’s name recovered the right email address no more than 1.24% of the time, but with the domain supplied, the rate climbed to 16.55%, and to 37.06% after five examples. Other factors, including how often an address appeared in the training data and whether surrounding email text came along with it, pushed the rate higher.

Deleting chat records isn’t a remedy, either. Several state attorneys general said deleting chat records may not undo their influence on trained models. And Common Sense Media’s Robbie Torney claimed that exporting or deleting your data “may not mean that that data is gone from model training.”

Note that people not only enter personal information about themselves during AI chats, but about their co-workers, friends, and relatives.

The main thing standing between your secrets and the world is company practice. We depend on the AI companies to keep our information private.

So what happens when those companies sell their assets?

## When AI bubbles burst

Online chatter about the “AI bubble” bursting is pretty much constant.

In China, the AI bubble has already burst, according to Reuters . Over the past few months, Chinese AI stocks have been pummeled.

Reuters reported that Shanghai’s STAR50 index of tech stocks fell 40% from its July high in under four months, erasing about $480 billion in market value, and that the broader CSI300 is down about 20% from its June highs.

It’s not a total collapse, but it does put pressure on US stock prices and also provides an incentive to transfer ownership through sales or mergers (though this hasn’t happened in China yet).

Still, the future is unknowable. Which AI companies will go bust as Character.AI did, get sold off, or get hacked?

As for the chatbots themselves, their inner workings are also unknowable.

That’s why we should all listen to the most paranoid amongst us, and never put sensitive information into chatbots. We just can’t trust AI to keep our secrets.
